## In Praise of Wandering

There is a particular kind of thinking that happens only when you are not trying to think. It arrives uninvited, usually when the mind has been given permission to drift, when the task is simply to walk and let the world present itself. This is not the disciplined thinking of the classroom or the workplace, not the focused problem-solving that we are so often taught to value. It is softer, more diffident, and yet in many ways it is the more fertile of the two. It is the thinking that happens in the margins, in the gaps between intention and action, when you are looking at nothing in particular and suddenly see everything.

I have always been drawn to walking. As a child, I would wander the woods behind my house not because I was going anywhere, but because the woods themselves were the destination. There was a creek that I knew from every angle, a fallen log that served as a bridge, a cluster of ferns that seemed to grow larger every week. I did not have a name for what I was doing, but I was practicing a kind of attention that would become more and more precious to me as I grew older. I was learning, without knowing it, that the world is not a backdrop to our lives but a participant in them, and that the more closely you look, the more the world looks back.

Now I live in a city, where walking is different. The streets are structured, the paths are paved, and there is little in the way of wilderness. But I have discovered that the same mode of attention works here. If I slow down, if I let my gaze loosen and my pace soften, the urban environment reveals its own kind of life. There is a particular tree on a particular corner that blooms a pale pink for exactly three weeks every spring, and I have come to know its schedule. There is a crack in the sidewalk that has become a small garden of dandelions and clover. There is a man who sits on the same bench every afternoon, feeding sparrows from his hand, and though we have never spoken, we greet each other with a nod. These are not the grand wonders of the natural world, but they are wonders nonetheless. They are evidence that attention is a kind of love, and that love is a kind of seeing.

The modern world is not friendly to this kind of attention. It is designed to capture and redirect our gaze, to flatten our experience into a series of stimuli that demand immediate response. Our devices buzz and blink; our feeds are infinite and engineered to keep us scrolling; our attention is a commodity to be harvested and sold. It is no wonder that so many of us feel scattered, anxious, exhausted. We are being pulled in a thousand directions at once, and the quiet interior space that once allowed for wandering thought has been colonized by notifications. The result is a paradox: we are more connected than ever, and yet we are less able to truly connect with the world in front of us. We see it through the lens of a photograph we will never look at again; we experience it in anticipation of sharing it; we are always elsewhere, even when we are here.

I catch myself doing this all the time. I will be walking along the river, and the light will be extraordinary, a low golden angle that turns the water into a sheet of moving glass, and my first instinct will be to reach for my phone. I want to capture it, to preserve it, to make it shareable. But something in me has learned to pause. I leave the phone in my pocket and simply look. The moment passes, as all moments do, and I have no record of it except the one in my memory. That memory, I have found, is stronger than any photograph. It is richer, more textured, alive with the feeling of the wind and the sound of the water and the particular quality of the light. It is not just an image; it is an experience, and it belongs to me in a way that no digital file ever could.

This is not to say that I am against technology. I am writing these words on a computer, and I will likely share them with you through some kind of screen. Technology has given us incredible things: access to information, connection across distance, tools for creation and collaboration that would have seemed like magic to previous generations. But technology, like any tool, shapes the one who uses it. It is not neutral. It carries with it a set of assumptions about time, attention, and value, and if we are not careful, we absorb those assumptions without ever questioning them. We begin to believe that productivity is the highest good, that every moment must be optimized, that the best response to anything is the quickest one. We forget that there is value in slowness, in repetition, in duration. We forget that some of our deepest insights come not when we are pushing toward a goal but when we are simply open to whatever comes.

William James once wrote that “my experience is what I agree to attend to.” This is a profound and unsettling idea. It means that we are not passive recipients of the world; we are active participants in the construction of our own reality. The universe is infinitely rich, infinitely complex, and we cannot take it all in. We must choose where to direct our attention, and those choices, made moment by moment, day by day, shape who we are. If I spend my days scrolling through images of other people’s lives, I will come to believe that my own life is somehow diminished by comparison. If I spend my days looking for the beautiful and the strange in my immediate surroundings, I will find it, and I will be richer for the finding. Attention is not just a cognitive act; it is a moral one. It is how we decide what matters.

I have been trying to practice a kind of attention that is less self-centered, more receptive. It is a way of looking that does not impose my own expectations on the world but allows the world to reveal itself on its own terms. This sounds mystical, but it is actually quite simple. It means walking without a destination. It means sitting on a park bench and watching the same patch of ground for ten minutes, noticing how the light shifts and the insects move and the grass bends in the wind. It means listening to a piece of music without doing anything else, letting it fill the space of the room and the space of the mind. It means being fully present to what is before me, even if what is before me is perfectly ordinary.

And the ordinary, I have found, is inexhaustible. A cup of coffee, a window with rain running down it, a distant siren, a conversation overheard in a café: each of these is a doorway to a world. The trick is to stop long enough to walk through. There is a practice in some contemplative traditions of doing things as if you have never done them before, of seeing a familiar object with fresh eyes. When I manage to do this, the world becomes strange and wonderful again. A tree is not just a tree but a kind of towering, branching organism that has been alive for decades, that has weathered storms and droughts and the careless passing of countless humans. A face is not just a face but a landscape of experience, every line and scar and expression holding a story I will never fully know. There is a depth to everything, if only we are willing to look.

But we are not often willing. We are in a hurry. We have places to go and people to see and lists of tasks that never seem to get shorter. Even our leisure has become frantic; we are constantly in search of the next thing, the better thing, the thing that will finally satisfy us. And yet it never does. The satisfaction we seek is not in the next thing but in the present thing, if only we could stop long enough to receive it. This is the deepest irony of the modern condition: we have more than ever before, and we enjoy it less. We are like diners at an endless feast, but we have forgotten how to taste.

I do not want to live that way. I want to be the kind of person for whom a single leaf is enough to justify an entire afternoon. I want to be the kind of person who can find infinite complexity in the face of someone I love. I want to be the kind of person whose attention is a gift, not a commodity. This is not easy. The pulls of distraction are strong, and I am weak. But I have noticed that the more I practice attention, the easier it becomes. It is like a muscle, or perhaps a habit, or perhaps a grace that is cultivated through repetition. Every time I choose to look without looking for something, every time I choose to listen without listening for something, I am strengthening a different kind of connection, not just to the world but to myself.

There is a moment that I return to often, a memory that has become almost luminous with significance. It happened on a cool autumn afternoon, somewhere in the countryside, on a walk I had taken many times before. I was not thinking about anything in particular. My mind was quiet, or as quiet as it ever gets, and I was simply there, following the path as it curved through the trees. At a certain point, I looked up and saw the light coming through the leaves in a way that I can only describe as holy. The leaves were gold and orange and red, and the sun was low enough to shine through them, setting them ablaze with color. The whole canopy seemed to be glowing from within. I stopped. I did not reach for my phone, and I did not try to analyze what I was seeing. I just stood there, breathing, and let the beauty wash over me. And I felt, for just a moment, that I was not separate from the world but part of it, that the same energy that was making the leaves glow was flowing through me as well. That moment has stayed with me for years. It cost nothing. It was not planned. It was simply a gift of attention.

I think that is what I am trying to cultivate in my life: the ability to receive gifts. This sounds simple, but it is actually quite difficult. Much of our culture is oriented around production, around making and achieving and acquiring. We are taught that value comes from what we do, not from what we receive. We are taught that we must be constantly active, constantly productive, constantly justified. But attention is not productive in that sense. It does not produce anything you can hold or sell or show off. It is a kind of passive openness, a willingness to be changed by what we encounter. And yet I have found that this passive openness is far more generative than any amount of forced effort. When I am most attentive, ideas come to me unbidden. Solutions to problems I have been wrestling with appear, seemingly out of nowhere. The connections between disparate things become visible. Attention, paradoxically, is not a distraction from creativity but a condition of it. I do not have a great idea by trying to have one; I have a great idea by making room for it, by being quiet enough to hear it when it arrives.

The writer and naturalist John Burroughs said, “I go to nature to be soothed and healed, and to have my senses put in order.” That is exactly what I feel when I am in the presence of something larger and older than myself, whether it is a forest or an ocean or simply a sky full of stars. I am not soothed because I escape my problems; I am soothed because I am reminded of my place in the great web of being. My problems are still there, but they seem smaller in proportion to the mystery. My time is still limited, but it seems less of a constraint when I am surrounded by the evidence of deep time, the long slow processes that have shaped the hills and carved the rivers. I am part of that. I am not a stranger here. I am a visitor, but a visitor who has been invited, and the invitation is renewed every time I pay attention.

In the end, perhaps that is the whole thing. The world is inviting us, at every moment, to look, to listen, to attend. The invitation is always open. But we must show up. We must leave our screens and our schedules and our endless mental chatter long enough to say yes. We must become, again, like children, who do not need a reason to stare at an ant or to feel the grass under their feet. We must recover the sense that we are not observers of the world but participants in it, and that our attention is not a resource to be managed but a gift to be offered.

I am not always good at this. There are days when I fall into the same loops of distraction as anyone else, days when my mind is a pinball machine of thoughts and worries and desires. But I have learned that those days do not last forever. There is always another walk, another sunset, another ordinary moment that becomes extraordinary if I am present enough to notice. The world is patient. It will wait for me. And that, I think, is the most generous thing about it. The world does not demand my attention; it simply offers it, over and over, like a friend who never grows tired of calling my name.

So I will keep wandering. I will keep walking without destination, looking without agenda, listening without hurry. I will keep trying to be a person who can sit still and watch a cloud change shape for an hour, who can find wonder in a puddle of rainwater, who can be fully present to the one small life I have been given. I will not always succeed. But I will keep trying, because the trying itself has become a kind of reward. In a world that is always pulling me toward the next thing, the most radical act I can think of is to be fully here, in this moment, attending to what is before me. And in that attention, I find not just peace but a kind of joy, a quiet and persistent joy that does not depend on circumstances. It is the joy of being awake, of being alive, of having been given the chance to see the light through the leaves, to hear the rain on the roof, to feel the warmth of another hand in mine. These are the things that matter. These are the things we will remember, if we are paying attention.

The French philosopher Simone Weil wrote that “attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.” To attend to something or someone is to say, you are worth my time, you are worth my presence, you are worth the stillness of my mind. This is not only a gift to the recipient; it is a gift to ourselves. Because when we give our attention, we become more alive. We become more ourselves. We step out of the shallow end of experience and into the depths, where the real treasures are hidden, where the ordinary world reveals its secret radiance. I do not know why this is. I do not know why beauty should be so closely tied to attention, or why presence should be so healing. I only know that it is true. I only know that the times in my life when I have felt most fully awake have been the times when I was most fully attentive, when I was not in a hurry, not reaching for the next thing, but simply and completely there.

So this is my small manifesto, though I hesitate to call it that. It is more like a reminder, a note to myself, pinned above the desk of my own consciousness: Pay attention. Be present. Do not rush past the miracle. The miracle is not in some distant place or future time; it is here, now, in the shape of a leaf, the sound of a distant train, the face of the person across the table. The miracle is in the waiting world, and the world is always waiting, always offering. The only question is whether I will be patient enough to receive it. I want to be. I am learning. And the learning, the slow turning of the heart toward what is real and true and beautiful, is the best thing I know. It is the reason I walk. It is the reason I write. It is the reason I am here, with you, attending to this small moment of connection, hoping that it matters.

It does matter. Everything does. We just have to look.
